subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: The counting-house opens onto a narrow court, and the weather that day is foggy and bitterly cold.
quote: although the court was of the narrowest, the houses opposite were mere phantoms
why: Weather and fog of the moment are sensory texture. The narrow court is a lasting layout detail but is only incidental here.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: The counting-house has neighbouring offices across the court whose windows show candles lit.
quote: candles were flaring in the windows of the neighbouring offices
why: Candles in the neighbouring windows are one-moment set dressing.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: Scrooge leaves the door of his counting-house open so he can keep his eye on his clerk.
quote: The door of Scrooge's counting-house was open that he might keep his eye upon his clerk
why: The open door is staging for this scene, though it shows Scrooge's supervision habit. The habit itself is not a stated rule.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Cratchit's comforter is white.
quote: the clerk put on his white comforter
why: The comforter is a momentary costume detail. It is a minor detail a later scene might repeat, but nothing hinges on it.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Cratchit applauded Fred's speech involuntarily and was immediately sensible of the impropriety.
quote: The clerk in the Tank involuntarily applauded.
why: A momentary reaction, involuntary applause and embarrassment. It is staging inside the scene.

subject: first-portly-gentleman
statement: Two portly gentlemen, collecting for charity, enter Scrooge's office just after Fred leaves; they carry books and papers and are visiting the firm for the first time, not knowing whether Scrooge or Marley is alive.
quote: This lunatic, in letting Scrooge's nephew out, had let two other people in. They were portly gentlemen, pleasant to behold
why: Staging of the collectors' entrance and appearance, plus a narrator aside; the in-scene arrival is not carried forward.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: Labourers are repairing the gas-pipes in the main street at the corner of the court, and have lit a great fire in a brazier around which ragged men and boys gather.
quote: In the main street, at the corner of the court, some labourers were repairing the gas-pipes, and had lighted a great fire in a brazier
why: A brazier fire and a gas-pipe repair crew are scenery of the moment, not a lasting state.

statement: The fog and darkness thicken and the cold intensifies as Christmas Eve afternoon goes on, after the charity collectors have left.
quote: Meanwhile the fog and darkness thickened so
why: Fog and cold thickening is the weather of the moment, which the story is unlikely to return to.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: A boy (a carol singer) stooped at Scrooge's keyhole to sing a Christmas carol, 'God bless you, merry gentleman! May nothing you dismay!', and fled in terror when Scrooge seized the ruler.
quote: Scrooge seized the ruler with such energy of action, that the singer fled in terror
why: The carol singer at the keyhole and his flight is in-scene staging and a momentary reaction.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Cratchit snuffed out his candle and put on his hat when Scrooge signalled closing time, ending his candle-warmth in the Tank for the day.
quote: who instantly snuffed his candle out, and put on his hat
why: Snuffing the candle and putting on his hat is staging in the moment as he leaves.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: The counting-house was closed up very quickly once Scrooge left.
quote: The office was closed in a twinkling
why: How quickly the office closed is a momentary description with no lasting content.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: After dinner Scrooge read all the newspapers and looked over his banker's-book for the rest of the evening before going home to bed.
quote: having read all the newspapers, and beguiled the rest of the evening with his banker's-book, went home to bed
why: What he did with the evening (newspapers, banker's-book) is a one-off activity that fills the evening, though it ends in going home to bed.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: The house has a black old gateway, around which fog and frost hang thickly on this night.
quote: The fog and frost so hung about the black old gateway of the house
why: The fog and frost around the gateway is the weather of the moment, which is atmospheric texture; the gateway itself is covered by other facts.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's face in the knocker is livid, lit by a dismal light, with ghostly spectacles pushed up on its forehead, hair stirred as if by breath, and wide-open motionless eyes; it looks at Scrooge as Marley used to look.
quote: with ghostly spectacles turned up on its ghostly forehead. The hair was curiously stirred, as if by breath or hot air; and, though the eyes were wide open, they were perfectly motionless.
why: The face's momentary appearance in the knocker is a vision's staging and sensory texture, gone once it reverts.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge enters his chambers, locks the street door behind him, and goes upstairs carrying a lit candle (a tallow dip).
quote: He fastened the door, and walked across the hall, and up the stairs; slowly too: trimming his candle as he went.
why: Locking the door and walking upstairs with a candle is in-scene staging.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge has a heavy door to his rooms which he shuts after checking them.
quote: But before he shut his heavy door, he walked through his rooms to see that all was right.
why: Shutting the heavy door after checking is in-scene staging, though the door itself is minor.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge double-locked his door that night, which was not his custom.
quote: double-locked himself in, which was not his custom
why: A one-night action that is staging inside this scene. The remark that it was not his custom is covered by fact 2.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge took off his cravat and put on his nightcap, and sat before the fire to eat his gruel.
quote: he took off his cravat; put on his dressing-gown and slippers, and his nightcap; and sat down before the fire to take his gruel.
why: Evening routine and clothing in the moment. A later scene may mention the nightcap, but this is staging.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge sees Marley's head's likeness on every tile of the fireplace, as if shaped from his thoughts.
quote: there would have been a copy of old Marley's head on every one.
why: A figurative, hypothetical image ('if each tile had been blank...'). It is Scrooge's imagination in the moment.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge dismisses the apparition of Marley's face with the word 'Humbug!' and walks across the room.
quote: "Humbug!" said Scrooge; and walked across the room.
why: A momentary reaction and movement inside the scene. His dismissive 'Humbug' is a recurring trait, but this specific instance is staging.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: The disused bell swung and rang, and then every bell in the house rang, for what might have been half a minute or a minute before ceasing together.
quote: This might have lasted half a minute, or a minute, but it seemed an hour. The bells ceased as they had begun, together.
why: How long the ringing lasted is a momentary in-scene event, and the narrator says it only seemed an hour.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's ghost came up from the cellar, up the stairs and through the heavy door of Scrooge's rooms without pausing, and entered the room.
quote: it came on through the heavy door, and passed into the room before his eyes
why: The ghost's path up the stairs and through the door is staging within this scene.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge says he does not believe in the ghost, declaring it humbug, even as it approaches his door.
quote: "It's humbug still!" said Scrooge. "I won't believe it."
why: Scrooge's disbelief at this moment is a reaction that shifts as the scene goes on.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's ghost sits on the opposite side of the fireplace from Scrooge.
quote: the ghost sat down on the opposite side of the fireplace, as if he were quite used to it.
why: In-scene staging of where the ghost sits.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: The ghost's lower jaw drops down upon its breast when it removes the bandage from its head.
quote: the phantom taking off the bandage round its head, as if it were too warm to wear indoors, its lower jaw dropped down upon its breast!
why: Momentary staging of the jaw dropping when the bandage comes off; a one-time effect.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's ghost rebinds its head wrapper afterward, the jaws knocking its teeth together, and ends standing erect with its chain wound over and about its arm.
quote: the spectre took its wrapper from the table, and bound it round its head, as before.
why: In-scene staging at the end: rebinding the head wrapper, standing erect with the chain on its arm.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge cannot see his own chain, which Marley says he bears.
quote: he could see nothing.
why: Momentary perception in the scene; Scrooge cannot see his chain now, which is not a lasting state.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge has a toothpick in this scene, which he threatens to swallow as a test.
quote: You see this toothpick?" said Scrooge
why: Prop used in the scene as a test; staging, not a lasting possession.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's ghost left Scrooge's chambers through the raised window, joining the mournful lament and floating out into the night.
quote: The spectre, after listening for a moment, joined in the mournful dirge; and floated out upon the bleak, dark night.
why: Staging of the ghost's exit within the scene; the ghost's departure itself is carried by later events, but this detail is momentary.

subject: phantom-spirits
statement: The air over Scrooge's chambers was filled with phantoms moaning as they wandered in restless haste, all wearing chains like Marley's, some linked together, none free.
quote: Every one of them wore chains like Marley's Ghost; some few (they might be guilty governments) were linked together; none were free.
why: A one-time scene vision of phantoms in the air; scenery that fades and is not returned to.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: After the phantoms and their voices faded, the night became as it had been when Scrooge walked home, and Scrooge then closed the window.
quote: But they and their spirit voices faded together; and the night became as it had been when he walked home.
why: Sequence of events within the scene (phantoms fade, window closed); no lasting state.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: After the visit Scrooge tried to say "Humbug!" but stopped after the first syllable.
quote: He tried to say "Humbug!" but stopped at the first syllable.
why: A momentary reaction in the scene; his failed 'Humbug' is an in-the-moment feeling.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: A neighbouring church's chimes strike the four quarters and then the hour, and the bell tolled twelve when Scrooge woke.
quote: the chimes of a neighbouring church struck the four quarters
why: Church chimes striking the quarters and hour is in-scene sensory staging.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-past
statement: The Ghost's form fluctuates in distinctness, with its limbs and parts dissolving and returning, while its belt sparkles in varying parts.
quote: the figure itself fluctuated in its distinctness: being now a thing with one arm, now with one leg, now with twenty legs, now a pair of legs without a head, now a head without a body
why: Fluctuating distinctness is a momentary visual effect, close to figurative or sensory texture.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: The Ghost holds Scrooge's arm in a grasp he cannot resist, and Scrooge clasps its robe as the Spirit moves toward the window.
quote: The grasp, though gentle as a woman's hand, was not to be resisted. He rose: but finding that the Spirit made towards the window, clasped his robe in supplication.
why: Grasp and clasping the robe are in-scene staging.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: The temperature is well below freezing and frost covers the window of Scrooge's bedroom chamber.
quote: the thermometer a long way below freezing
why: Weather of the moment and frost on the window are sensory setting.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge holds a financial instrument: a bill of exchange payable 'three days after sight' to Mr. Ebenezer Scrooge or his order.
quote: "three days after sight of this First of Exchange pay to Mr. Ebenezer Scrooge or his order,"
why: The bill of exchange is a narrator's joking aside, not a real possession shown.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge and the Ghost passed through the wall of his chambers and now stand on an open country road with fields on either side, the city gone.
quote: they passed through the wall, and stood upon an open country road, with fields on either hand. The city had entirely vanished.
why: Staging of the transition and the vision's setting; where they stand in the moment is scenery.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-past
statement: The scene Scrooge is carried to is a clear, cold winter day with snow on the ground, unlike the dark misty night he left.
quote: it was a clear, cold, winter day, with snow upon the ground.
why: Weather and light inside the vision are set dressing; the vision's season is not a lasting fact.

subject: open-country-road-childhood-town
statement: The travelling boys, on ponies and in country gigs and carts driven by farmers, are going home for Christmas and wish each other Merry Christmas as they part at cross-roads and bye-ways.
quote: when he heard them give each other Merry Christmas, as they parted at cross-roads and bye-ways, for their several homes!
why: Scenery and staging inside the vision: boys traveling and exchanging greetings on that day.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: The school's stables hold fowls, and its coach-houses and sheds are overgrown with grass.
quote: Fowls clucked and strutted in the stables; and the coach-houses and sheds were over-run with grass.
why: Fowls in stables and grass-grown sheds are set dressing within a vision; low chance of being revisited.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: A long, bare schoolroom with plain deal forms and desks lies through a door at the back of the house, across the hall.
quote: a door at the back of the house. It opened before them, and disclosed a long, bare, melancholy room, made barer still by lines of plain deal forms and desks.
why: Room layout and furniture within a vision, seen once; staging detail.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: The school's grounds include a dull yard behind with a half-thawed water-spout and a lone despondent poplar with leafless boughs, plus a store-house with a swinging door.
quote: not a drip from the half-thawed water-spout in the dull yard behind, not a sigh among the leafless boughs of one despondent poplar, not the idle swinging of an empty store-house door
why: Yard, water-spout, poplar and store-house door are sensory scenery inside a vision.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: The boy Scrooge sits reading alone by a feeble fire in the schoolroom; his adult self weeps to see him.
quote: At one of these a lonely boy was reading near a feeble fire; and Scrooge sat down upon a form, and wept to see his poor forgotten self as he used to be.
why: Boy reading by a feeble fire and Scrooge sitting and weeping is in-vision staging and momentary reaction.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge recognises and names Ali Baba, Valentine and Orson, the Sultan's Groom, the Parrot, Robin Crusoe and Friday as figures from the stories he read as a boy.
quote: "Why, it's Ali Baba!" Scrooge exclaimed in ecstasy. "It's dear old honest Ali Baba!
why: Recognising the figures in the moment is a reaction within the vision; the lasting backstory is covered by fact 8.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge pities his former self, calling him 'Poor boy!'
quote: he said, in pity for his former self, "Poor boy!" and cried again.
why: Momentary feeling of pity and tears in the vision.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge dries his eyes with his cuff and puts his hand in his pocket, wishing to give something.
quote: putting his hand in his pocket, and looking about him, after drying his eyes with his cuff
why: Momentary gesture of drying eyes and reaching into his pocket; the lasting part is the wish in fact 12.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge leaves the school with Fan in a chaise, driven by the postboy, with his trunk tied on top.
quote: Master Scrooge's trunk being by this time tied on to the top of the chaise, the children bade the schoolmaster good-bye right willingly
why: Staging of the departure inside the vision: chaise, postboy, trunk. It is scenery and does not carry forward.

subject: fezziwigs-warehouse
statement: The housemaid came with her cousin, the baker, and the cook with her brother's particular friend, the milkman; also present were the boy from over the way and the girl from next door but one.
quote: In came the housemaid, with her cousin, the baker. In came the cook, with her brother's particular friend, the milkman.
why: Guest-list texture inside a vision. It is set dressing the story never returns to.

subject: boy-from-over-the-way
statement: The boy from over the way was suspected of not having board enough from his master, and the girl from next door but one had her ears pulled by her mistress.
quote: the boy from over the way, who was suspected of not having board enough from his master; trying to hide himself behind the girl from next door but one, who was proved to have had her ears pulled by her mistress.
why: Comic asides about minor guests, which are set dressing inside a vision.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-past
statement: The Ghost says its time with Scrooge is growing short.
quote: "My time grows short," observed the Spirit. "Quick!"
why: A momentary remark about time running short that applies only in this scene.

subject: belle
statement: Belle is a fair young girl who wears a mourning-dress when Scrooge is with her in this scene.
quote: sat by the side of a fair young girl in a mourning-dress
why: The mourning-dress is a costume detail of this vision. Belle's youth and fairness are incidental description.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: The young Scrooge asserts that he has not changed toward Belle and defends his pursuit of wealth as the world's own hypocrisy about poverty.
quote: I am not changed towards you.
why: Scrooge's in-the-moment protestation and rhetoric within the vision; the lasting content is covered by other facts.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge begs the Ghost to show him no more and to conduct him home, asking why it delights to torture him.
quote: "Spirit!" said Scrooge, "show me no more! Conduct me home. Why do you delight to torture me?"
why: Scrooge's plea is a momentary emotional reaction; it does not carry forward as a fact.

subject: belles-husband
statement: Belle's husband came home the same evening he saw Scrooge, bringing toys and presents for the children, carried by a porter.
quote: just in time to greet the father, who came home attended by a man laden with Christmas toys and presents
why: Husband coming home with toys carried by a porter is in-scene staging within a vision; the same-evening link is less critical than the knowledge fact.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-past
statement: The Ghost says the visions are shadows of the things that have been, and that it is not to be blamed for what they are.
quote: "I told you these were shadows of the things that have been," said the Ghost. "That they are what they are, do not blame me!"
why: The Ghost's remark is an in-the-moment reminder of what it already said; it's dialogue, not new lasting fact.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-past
statement: The Ghost's face in this moment shows fragments of all the faces it has shown Scrooge.
quote: a face, in which in some strange way there were fragments of all the faces it had shown him
why: The Ghost's momentary face showing fragments is a fleeting visual detail.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge drew aside every one of his bed curtains with his own hands and lay down again keeping watch all round the bed.
quote: he put them every one aside with his own hands; and lying down again, established a sharp look-out all round the bed.
why: In-scene staging: curtains drawn and watch kept, which doesn't carry past the scene.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge intends to challenge the Spirit the moment it appears and does not want to be taken by surprise.
quote: he wished to challenge the Spirit on the moment of its appearance, and did not wish to be taken by surprise
why: A momentary intention that the scene itself immediately overturns when no spirit appears; later scenes won't hold it to this.

subject: scrooges-bedroom
statement: When the clock struck One, a blaze of ruddy light streamed onto Scrooge's bed, with Scrooge at its centre.
quote: he lay upon his bed, the very core and centre of a blaze of ruddy light, which streamed upon it when the clock proclaimed the hour
why: Sensory and set-dressing detail of the light on the bed, specific to this moment.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge got out of bed and shuffled in his slippers to the door of the adjoining room, and put his hand on the lock.
quote: he got up softly and shuffled in his slippers to the door.
why: Staging of movement within the scene: getting up, shuffling to the door, hand on the lock.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: Scrooge's room is hung with living green: holly, mistletoe and ivy cover the walls and ceiling, with bright berries among them.
quote: The walls and ceiling were so hung with living green, that it looked a perfect grove; from every part of which, bright gleaming berries glistened.
why: Room decoration is set dressing for this scene; the greenery is the Spirit's staging and the story doesn't rely on it later.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-present
statement: The Ghost of Christmas Present sits on a throne-like heap of food on Scrooge's floor: turkeys, geese, game, poultry, brawn, joints of meat, sucking-pigs, sausages, mince-pies, plum-puddings, oysters, chestnuts, apples, oranges, pears, twelfth-cakes and bowls of punch.
quote: Heaped up on the floor, to form a kind of throne, were turkeys, geese, game, poultry, brawn, great joints of meat, sucking-pigs, long wreaths of sausages, mince-pies, plum-puddings, barrels of oysters, red-hot chestnuts, cherry-cheeked apples, juicy oranges, luscious pears, immense twelfth-cakes, and seething bowls of punch
why: The food throne is scene-bound set dressing and is not carried forward.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge enters the Spirit's presence timidly and with his head hung, no longer the dogged Scrooge he had been, and does not like to meet the Spirit's eyes.
quote: He was not the dogged Scrooge he had been; and though the Spirit's eyes were clear and kind, he did not like to meet them.
why: Scrooge's timid manner and downcast eyes are a reaction in the moment, not a lasting state.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: On Christmas morning the townspeople scrape snow from the pavements in front of their dwellings and from their housetops, and the poulterers' shops are still half open.
quote: The poulterers' shops were still half open
why: Street scenery and shop staging in this vision of the moment; set dressing the story won't return to.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: On Christmas morning the Grocers' shops are nearly closed, with perhaps one or two shutters down, while customers crowd in.
quote: nearly closed, with perhaps two shutters down, or one
why: Sensory scenery of grocers' shops in the vision; momentary set dressing.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge accuses the Spirit, in effect, of seeking to close bakers' shops on the Seventh Day, which would deprive the poor of their only real dinner of the week, and says it has been done in the spirits' name or that of their family.
quote: You would deprive them of their means of dining every seventh day, often the only day on which they can be said to dine at all
why: This is Scrooge's accusation within the dialogue and a momentary argument; the content is largely the narrator-level framing of his charge. The Spirit denies it, and it does not become a lasting state.

subject: peter-cratchit
statement: Peter wears a monstrous shirt collar that is Bob's private property, lent for Christmas Day.
quote: the corners of his monstrous shirt collar (Bob's private property, conferred upon his son and heir in honour of the day)
why: Borrowed collar is Christmas Day set dressing and a passing comic detail, not carried forward.

subject: mrs-cratchit
statement: Mrs. Cratchit wears a twice-turned gown trimmed with cheap ribbons.
quote: dressed out but poorly in a twice-turned gown, but brave in ribbons, which are cheap and make a goodly show for sixpence
why: Her dress and ribbons are costume texture for the day; the lasting poverty is covered elsewhere.

subject: martha-cratchit
statement: Martha saw a countess and a lord some days before, and says the lord was about as tall as Peter.
quote: how she had seen a countess and a lord some days before, and how the lord "was much about as tall as Peter;"
why: A passing anecdote of the lord's height is trivia, not something later scenes depend on.

subject: tiny-tim
statement: Tiny Tim has a plaintive little voice and sang a song about a lost child travelling in the snow.
quote: a song, about a lost child travelling in the snow, from Tiny Tim, who had a plaintive little voice
why: A one-time song and a voice description; the song is a momentary performance.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge is overcome with penitence and grief on hearing the Ghost quote his own words about the surplus population back at him.
quote: Scrooge hung his head to hear his own words quoted by the Spirit, and was overcome with penitence and grief.
why: An emotional reaction in the moment.

subject: cratchit-home-camden-town
statement: The Cratchits' Christmas dinner is a goose with apple-sauce and mashed potatoes, followed by a pudding; the goose was just sufficient for the whole family.
quote: Eked out by apple-sauce and mashed potatoes, it was a sufficient dinner for the whole family
why: The meal's menu is a one-time event; its details are scene texture.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Bob took Tiny Tim to church on Christmas morning, carrying him on his shoulder and running home with him "all the way from church".
quote: for he had been Tim's blood horse all the way from church, and had come home rampant
why: The journey from church is a momentary event of the morning, not a lasting state.

subject: desolate-moor
statement: The moor is bleak and desert, strewn with monstrous masses of rude stone, with water held prisoner by frost and nothing growing but moss, furze and coarse rank grass.
quote: they stood upon a bleak and desert moor, where monstrous masses of rude stone were cast about, as though it were the burial-place of giants
why: Scenery of the moor inside a vision; set dressing the story does not return to.

subject: desolate-moor
statement: The sun sets in the west as the Ghost and Scrooge arrive on the moor, and night falls fully while they are there.
quote: Down in the west the setting sun had left a streak of fiery red
why: Sunset and nightfall are the momentary light of this one vision scene.

subject: miners-hut
statement: The miners' hut has walls of mud and stone, which Scrooge and the Spirit pass through to enter.
quote: Passing through the wall of mud and stone, they found a cheerful company assembled round a glowing fire.
why: Wall material and passing through it is staging and set dressing inside a vision.

subject: lighthouse-keepers
statement: The elder lighthouse keeper has a face damaged and scarred by hard weather and sings a sturdy song.
quote: the elder, too, with his face all damaged and scarred with hard weather
why: The elder keeper's scarred face and his song are a one-off description of a minor figure in a vision, not returned to.

subject: lighthouse
statement: The lighthouse has thick stone walls with a loophole through which the keepers' firelight shows onto the sea.
quote: through the loophole in the thick stone wall shed out a ray of brightness on the awful sea
why: The loophole and firelight are set dressing of the lighthouse interior in a vision.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: The Ghost and Scrooge travel by air from the moor out over the sea, and Scrooge holds the Ghost's robe during the journey.
quote: bade Scrooge hold his robe, and passing on above the moor, sped
why: In-scene travel staging (holding the robe, flying over the sea) is moment-to-moment movement.

subject: topper
statement: Topper sings bass in the family's glees and catches without swelling the veins in his forehead or reddening.
quote: especially Topper, who could growl away in the bass like a good one
why: Narrator's aside about how Topper performs in the music; a minor in-scene detail, though his bass singing is mild.

subject: freds-house
statement: About twenty people, young and old, are at Fred's party.
quote: There might have been twenty people there, young and old
why: Headcount at the party is staging inside a vision, not something carried forward.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-present
statement: The Ghost of Christmas Present keeps two children, a boy and a girl, hidden in the folds of its robe, from which it brings them out.
quote: From the foldings of its robe, it brought two children; wretched, abject, frightful, hideous, miserable.
why: Where the children were hidden is staging inside the scene.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-present
statement: The Spirit visited many homes and lands, including sick beds, almshouses, hospitals and jails, and left his blessing wherever he was not barred out.
quote: In almshouse, hospital, and jail, in misery's every refuge, where vain man in his little brief authority had not made fast the door, and barred the Spirit out, he left his blessing
why: This is a summary of what the visit passed over, a vision of the visit's scenery.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge follows the Phantom, moving in the shadow of its dress, which seems to bear him up and carry him along; the two leave this spot together.
quote: Scrooge followed in the shadow of its dress, which bore him up, he thought, and carried him along.
why: Following in the shadow of its dress is in-scene staging and movement, and the sensation of being carried is momentary.

subject: london-exchange-business-district
statement: The merchants gather on 'Change, where they hurry up and down, chink money in their pockets, converse in groups, consult their watches and toy with great gold seals.
quote: on 'Change, amongst the merchants; who hurried up and down, and chinked the money in their pockets, and conversed in groups, and looked at their watches, and trifled thoughtfully with their great gold seals
why: Generic set dressing of the Exchange crowd's behavior in this vision; texture, not a lasting state.

subject: red-faced-gentleman-with-the-pendulous-nose
statement: The red-faced gentleman has a pendulous excrescence on the end of his nose that shakes like the gills of a turkey-cock.
quote: a red-faced gentleman with a pendulous excrescence on the end of his nose, that shook like the gills of a turkey-cock
why: Physical description of a minor character in a vision, used as comic texture. Figurative simile, but it could return as an identifying trait; the vision scenery leans non-persisting.

subject: london-exchange-business-district
statement: The two men's conversation takes place on a cold morning, seasonable for Christmas time, and one of them says 'Good morning!' at parting.
quote: "Seasonable for Christmas time. You're not a skater, I suppose?"
why: Weather and time of day inside a vision are scenery and staging, and the greeting is momentary.

subject: london-exchange-business-district
statement: The two men's whole exchange is one brief meeting, a few lines of conversation, and a parting, with nothing more said.
quote: Not another word. That was their meeting, their conversation, and their parting.
why: This is the content and brevity of a single exchange inside a vision, which is staging.

subject: london-exchange-business-district
statement: Scrooge has an accustomed corner at the Exchange, which another man now occupies, and the clock points to his usual time of day for being there.
quote: another man stood in his accustomed corner, and though the clock pointed to his usual time of day for being there
why: This is vision scenery. Another man in his corner and the clock reading are staging within the vision.

subject: old-joes-rag-and-bone-shop
statement: The shop buys iron, old rags, bottles, bones and greasy offal, and its floor is piled with rusty keys, nails, chains, hinges, files, scales, weights and refuse iron.
quote: where iron, old rags, bottles, bones, and greasy offal, were bought
why: Shop inventory and floor clutter is set dressing within the vision.

subject: old-joes-rag-and-bone-shop
statement: The shop door's hinges are rusty and screech, and Joe's parlour is the space behind the screen of rags.
quote: The parlour was the space behind the screen of rags.
why: Hinge screech and parlour layout is staging and set dressing inside the vision.

subject: old-joe
statement: Joe asked whether the man died of anything catching, and the charwoman said he did not.
quote: I hope he didn't die of anything catching? Eh?
why: A passing question and answer about contagion; it does not carry beyond the scene.

subject: old-joe
statement: Joe paid out the gains from a flannel bag of money, telling the sums out on the ground.
quote: old Joe, producing a flannel bag with money in it, told out their several gains upon the ground
why: Staging detail of how Joe paid out the money.

subject: dead-mans-dark-chamber
statement: The body lies on a bare, uncurtained bed in the dead man's chamber, covered by a ragged sheet.
quote: a bare, uncurtained bed: on which, beneath a ragged sheet, there lay a something covered up
why: Bed and sheet are staging and set dressing inside a vision of the room, not returned to as a lasting state.

subject: dead-mans-dark-chamber
statement: A cat is tearing at the door of the death-room and rats gnaw beneath the hearth-stone.
quote: A cat was tearing at the door, and there was a sound of gnawing rats beneath the hearth-stone.
why: The cat and rats are sensory texture of the room in the vision, not carried forward.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge tells the Spirit he understands what it wants (to uncover the face) but lacks the power to do it.
quote: "I understand you," Scrooge returned, "and I would do it, if I could. But I have not the power, Spirit. I have not the power."
why: Scrooge's statement of inability is a momentary reaction within the scene, not a lasting state.

subject: debtor-familys-home
statement: The scene takes place by daylight, with the dinner kept warm by the fire for the husband.
quote: revealed a room by daylight, where a mother and her children were
why: The daylight and the dinner by the fire are scene staging and set dressing inside a vision.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-yet-to-come
statement: The Phantom shows Scrooge a room in which the household is made happier by the dead creditor's death; the only emotion it can show him connected with the death is pleasure.
quote: The only emotion that the Ghost could show him, caused by the event, was one of pleasure.
why: This is narrator commentary on the vision's emotional content, a reaction in the moment rather than a lasting fact.

subject: peter-cratchit
statement: Peter Cratchit reads aloud from a book to the family; he reads the Bible verse about a child set in the midst of them.
quote: sat looking up at Peter, who had a book before him.
why: Peter reading aloud is staging inside the vision, not a lasting trait.

subject: mrs-cratchit
statement: Mrs. Cratchit's eyes are weak and the colour of the sewing hurts them by candle-light; she hides weak eyes from Bob.
quote: "The colour hurts my eyes," she said.
why: Her eyes hurting from the colour is a momentary reaction inside the vision.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: The scene takes place in the evening, around Bob's usual time of coming home from work, by candle-light.
quote: It makes them weak by candle-light; and I wouldn't show weak eyes to your father when he comes home, for the world. It must be near his time.
why: The evening setting and Bob's near arrival time are staging inside the vision.

subject: mrs-cratchit
statement: Mrs. Cratchit and her daughters are sewing work that will be finished long before Sunday.
quote: They would be done long before Sunday, he said.
why: The sewing and its completion before Sunday is scenery inside the vision.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Bob wears his comforter at home, as he has need of it.
quote: little Bob in his comforter --he had need of it, poor fellow--came in.
why: Bob's comforter is incidental set dressing.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: In the future vision, Scrooge's office is still an office but no longer his: the furniture is different and another figure sits in the chair.
quote: It was an office still, but not his. The furniture was not the same, and the figure in the chair was not himself.
why: Furniture and the figure in the chair are staging inside a future vision; the only lasting point is that the business changed hands, which the scene does not develop.

subject: churchyard
statement: The churchyard is entered through an iron gate; it is walled in by houses, overrun with grass and weeds, and choked with too much burying.
quote: until they reached an iron gate.
why: The gate and the look of the churchyard are scenery inside a vision, and the narrator's description of the place is mostly aside.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-yet-to-come
statement: During the confrontation the Ghost's hand appears to shake and tremble, and it repulses Scrooge when he catches its hand.
quote: For the first time the hand appeared to shake.
why: The Ghost's trembling hand is a momentary reaction and staging within the scene.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge's bed-curtains are still hanging, rings and all, and were not torn down.
quote: they are not torn down, rings and all.
why: The bed-curtains still hanging is a momentary staging detail in the scene; it does not carry forward.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge is dressing himself in day garments and stockings, turning some inside out and putting them on upside down, tearing some and mislaying others.
quote: His hands were busy with his garments all this time; turning them inside out, putting them on upside down, tearing them, mislaying them, making them parties to every kind of extravagance.
why: His fumbling with clothes is in-the-moment business and a passing reaction; it has no lasting effect.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge knows Tiny Tim's size well enough to judge the turkey twice as big as him.
quote: It's twice the size of Tiny Tim.
why: Figurative comparison of the turkey's size to Tiny Tim, a joke and exaggeration; it states no lasting fact.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge wrote the turkey's delivery address himself, with an unsteady hand.
quote: The hand in which he wrote the address was not a steady one, but write it he did, somehow
why: In-the-moment staging, a shaky hand while writing the address; the lasting facts (address, delivery) are covered elsewhere.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge recognises the portly gentleman on sight in the street and expects the old gentleman to look upon him badly because of the earlier refusal.
quote: It sent a pang across his heart to think how this old gentleman would look upon him when they met
why: Scrooge's anticipated pang and expectation of disapproval is a momentary feeling and reaction in this scene.

subject: first-portly-gentleman
statement: The portly gentleman addresses him as "Mr. Scrooge" as a question, uncertain at first that it is the same man.
quote: "Mr. Scrooge?"
why: The gentleman's questioning tone is a momentary reaction of surprise within the scene.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge spends his Christmas walk attending church and wandering the streets, patting children on the head and questioning beggars, and finds that everything yields him pleasure.
quote: He went to church, and walked about the streets, and watched the people hurrying to and fro, and patted children on the head, and questioned beggars
why: Details of his walk and the pleasure he took in it are in-scene texture; the lasting change is his redemption, which is covered elsewhere.

subject: freds-house
statement: Fred's house has a dining-room, where Fred and his wife are inspecting the table when Scrooge arrives.
quote: They were looking at the table (which was spread out in great array)
why: The dining-room and the couple inspecting the table are staging and set dressing for this scene.

subject: fred
statement: Fred did not expect Scrooge's visit and does not at first know who is at the door.
quote: "Why bless my soul!" cried Fred, "who's that?"
why: Fred's surprise is a momentary reaction, though the fact that he was not expecting the visit could be kept, the lasting piece (the visit being unannounced) is minor.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Bob Cratchit believes Scrooge has gone mad, thinking of knocking him down with the ruler and calling for a strait-waistcoat.
quote: He had a momentary idea of knocking Scrooge down with it, holding him, and calling to the people in the court for help and a strait-waistcoat.
why: Bob's momentary fear and passing idea is an in-the-moment reaction, though what he believes about Scrooge could matter, it is a fleeting reaction.
